look_here_first: Look at the overall frond architecture: pinnae spread in a broad, fanlike or horseshoe arrangement from the upper end of a slender dark stipe. Contrast this with the elongated, repeatedly branching triangular fronds of the locally relevant Adiantum capillus-veneris; do not identify by black stalk alone.

project_inclusion.range_basis: B057 deep review: accepted Adiantum pedatum L.; Kew native range does not include Texas.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Do not count as confirmed Central Texas target-zone native. Northern maidenhair is retained as a learner comparison.

best_field_traits: Terrestrial rhizomatous perennial fern, not a flowering plant.
Slender glossy dark brown to black stipe; pinnae radiate or curve in a fanlike arrangement from the distal stipe.
Small asymmetrical fan- to wedge-shaped pinnules with repeatedly forked veins.
Fertile pinnule margins roll back to form false indusia over marginal sori.
Spore-bearing structures, not flowers or seeds, are the reproductive characters to inspect.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Frond branching pattern first; then fertile pinnule margins and pinna arrangement.

comparisons.key_distinctions: A. pedatum: broad horseshoe/fan arrangement of pinnae arising near the stipe apex; A. capillus-veneris: triangular to elongated, 1–3-pinnate frond with branching rachis, common around Central Texas moist limestone seeps. Both have dark stipes and marginal false indusia, so these shared characters do not separate them.
